title: Debates in the Dark; Instruction in the Light
author: Science of Reading Classroom
summary: Using a tutee named Sarah as a case, the author shows what isolated reading-strategy instruction looks like: each week a new skill or literary device, practised on short passages, with no books read at all. Sarah was bored and her ELA class was joyless. The author then turns to the online fight between Knowers, who prioritise knowledge and vocabulary building, and Strategists, who defend strategy instruction, and argues that the two camps mostly agree that both content and strategies are needed. The debates are unhelpful and are radicalizing teachers against either knowledge-building curricula or effective strategy instruction. The remedy is to ground arguments in classroom artifacts such as videos, worksheets, slides and assessments, so that debate is about what actually happens in classrooms.
points: Strategy instruction detached from sustained texts, as in Sarah's weekly skill-of-the-week ELA class, is boring and ineffective, whichever camp is critiquing it.
The knowledge-versus-strategies debate is largely a false split because neither side wants to eliminate strategies or make them the sole focus.
The online debate is actively harmful, pushing teachers toward extremes against knowledge-building curriculum or against effective strategy instruction.
Practical fix: bring concrete classroom artifacts to every argument so critique and praise are specific.
quotes: Sarah’s ELA class revolved around a new skill, strategy, or literary device each week. The teacher introduced it at the beginning of the week. They practiced applying it together in class and then independently for homework.

One side–“The Knowers”–contends that systematically building students' knowledge and vocabulary is key to producing more proficient readers and writers. They blame isolated strategy instruction–like Sarah’s ELA class–for stagnant or falling reading scores.

First, the participants in these debates mostly agree: No participant is advocating for eliminating strategy instruction. No participant believes that the strategies themselves should be the sole focus of teaching reading comprehension (as they were in Sarah’s 7th grade class).

Second, these debates are not helping teachers. They’re certainly not helping students learn to read better. In fact, if anything they’re radicalizing some teachers against knowledge-building curriculum, and they’re radicalizing other teachers against effective strategy instruction.

When we discuss and debate classroom practice, we should bring it into the light with artifacts and concrete examples from actual classrooms: videos, writing samples, assessments, worksheets, slides. I know that both sides would agree that what Sarah experienced in 7th grade ELA class was ineffective and soulless and joyless.

The next time you get into an argument, whether it’s about strategy instruction or something else, on X or in a Facebook Group, bring examples! Get specific about what you’re critiquing or praising or wondering.
